ety.text: From Middle English foyle, from Middle French fueille, from Old French fueille (“plant leaf”), from Late Latin folia, the plural of folium, mistaken as a singular feminine. The literary sense is from the practice of backing a gem with metal foil to make it shine more brilliantly. Doublet of folio and folium, distantly also with phyllo and phyllon.

ety.text: From Middle English foilen (“spoil a scent trail by crossing it”), from Old French fouler (“tread on, trample”), ultimately from Latin fullō (“to trample, full”).
From French foulis.
From mnemonic acronym FOIL (“First Outside Inside Last”).

senses.d: A very thin sheet of metal.
A very thin sheet of plastic.
Thin aluminium/aluminum (or, formerly, tin) used for wrapping food.
ex: wrap the sandwich up in foil

senses.d: A thin layer of metal put between a jewel and its setting to make it seem more brilliant.

In literature, theatre/theater, etc., a character who helps emphasize the traits of the main character and who usually acts as an opponent or antagonist, but can also serve as the sidekick of the protagonist.
Anything that acts by contrast to emphasise the characteristics of something.
ex:
1725-1726, William Broome, The Odyssey
Hector has also a foil to set regard
As she a black silk cap on him begun / To set, for foil of his milk-white to serve.

senses.d: A very thin sword with a blunted (or foiled) tip.
ex:
1784-1810, William Mitford, History of Greece
Socrates contended with a foil against Demosthenes with a sword.
Blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit, but hurt not.

senses.d: A thin, transparent plastic material on which marks are made and projected for the purposes of presentation. See transparency.
A premium trading card with a glossy finish.
ex: I personally would collect all the foils from Base Set before this one, but the market is what the market is.

senses.d: A stylized flower or leaf.
To cover or wrap with foil.
To prevent (something) from being accomplished.
To prevent (someone) from accomplishing something.
ex: I was foiled by my superior
And by mortal man at length am foil'd.

senses.d: To blunt; to dull; to spoil.
ex: they foil the scent of one another.

senses.d: To tread underfoot; to trample.
ex: King Richard […] caused the ensigns of Leopold to be pulled down and foiled underfoot.
Whom he did all to pieces breake and foyle, / In filthy durt, and left so in the loathely soyle.

senses.d: Failure when on the point of attainment; defeat; frustration; miscarriage.
ex: Fame is no plant that grows on mortal foil
Nor e'er was fate so near a foil.

senses.d: One of the incorrect answers presented in a multiple-choice test.
The track of an animal.
ex: […]but after giving her a dodge, here's another b— follows me upon the foil.

senses.d: To expand a product of two or more algebraic expressions, typically binomials.
To defile; to soil.
A small arc in the tracery of a window, etc.
